title: From the Garage to a win
text: Five steps, in the order you meet them.

title: Pick a tank
text: 01 The Garage opens on your fleet of 221 tanks. Pick one: its dossier shows the armour, the gun and how it moves, and the Tank Gallery opens its full anatomy.

title: Deploy
text: 02 Deploy sets the battle: one of 13 modes, a battlefield (or a random one of 31), the time of day, and the sides, 7 v 7 or 14 v 14.

title: Drive and aim
text: 03 W A S D drive; the mouse turns the turret. L-SHIFT drops into the gunner's sight at ×2 / ×4 / ×8, the wheel zooms, and CAPS holds the gun while you look around.

title: Fire
text: 04 LMB fires; hold it to fire at each reload. 1 2 3 pick the shell. 4 5 6 use the Repair Kit (35 s), the First Aid Kit (45 s) and the Fire Extinguisher (25 s); a kit's cooldown starts only once it has done something.

title: Win
text: 05 Standard Battle is won by destroying every enemy inside its 15-minute clock; every other mode sets its own goal. When you are knocked out, the camera follows your allies.

title: Next
text: Controls and Watch Every key, the touch layout and Watch mode's three views. Game modes Every mode's goal, clock and rules, drawn on the map.

title: How a shell becomes damage
text: Penetration, angles, modules and crew, and who sees whom, charted from the game's own rules.

title: Penetration
text: A shell goes through when its penetration, rolled 75–125 %, beats the armour it meets. 200 400 600 800 1000 100 500 1000 1500 2000 Range (m) mm OFL 120 F2 APFSDS OECC 120 F1 HEAT Penetration falls linearly from its 100 m figure to its 1,000 m figure, then on to 2,000 m where the shell has one. Penetration and damage each roll 75–125 % of their figure. HEAT keeps its penetration at any range.

title: Angling
text: Angle the plate and it gets thicker along the shell's path, until the shell bounces off. 100 200 300 400 500 0 15 30 45 60 75 Impact angle (°) mm AP, 75 mm bounces past 70° APCR, 75 mm bounces past 70° APFSDS, 120 mm bounces past 78° HEAT, 120 mm Effective armour is the plate divided by the cosine of the angle less the shell's normalization. APFSDS turns 2° toward the plate and bounces past 78°. AP turns 5° toward the plate and bounces past 70°. A shell 3× wider than the plate never bounces. A shell bounces at most 2 times; a HEAT jet dies on its first. Leclerc XLR: armour by thickness

title: Spaced armour, ERA and HE
text: Not every plate is solid steel, and not every shell needs to go through. Air gaps cost HEAT 5 % of its penetration per 10 cm. ERA takes a fixed bite out of HEAT and a share of a kinetic round; a tandem warhead goes through it unless the block is built against tandems. HE never bounces: it blasts what it hits, plate or not.

title: Modules and crew
text: A hit that goes through can break what is behind the plate. Broken modules repair themselves after 10 s. Leclerc XLR: modules and crew Module Hit points Chance to be hit Gun 150 33 % Turret ring 120 45 % Gun mount 120 45 % Autoloader 125 36 % Weapon feed 110 38 % Roof gun 80 65 % Missile rack 120 30 % Engine 160 45 % Transmission 140 45 % Fuel tank 120 45 % Ammo rack 150 27 % Radio 90 45 % Optics 80 45 % Track L 100 100 % Track R 100 100 % A damaged ammo rack slows the reload ×1.5; a destroyed one blows the tank up. A damaged engine catches fire 15 % of the time; a fire burns 10 ticks of 0.5 % hull and may go out by itself (12 % a tick). A shell that goes through hits a crew member 33 % of the time (10 % for HE splash); losing every crew member loses the tank. Damaged optics cut the view range by 50 %. A working radio shares what you see within 600 m; a damaged one within 300 m.

title: Spotting
text: You see a tank when it is inside your view range less its camo, between 50 m and 445 m. 100 200 300 400 500 0 10 20 30 40 50 60 Target camo (%) m 445 m view range 380 m view range 300 m view range Inside 50 m a tank is always seen, even through cover. A tank stays seen 5 s after the last sighting. The sixth-sense lamp lights 3 s after you are spotted and stays 8 s. Firing strips most of your camo for a moment; bushes near you turn see-through after you fire. Bushes and trees add up to 50 % camo; a camo paint that matches the map adds 3.5 %.

title: A browser game built through verified loops
text: Claude of Tanks grew from a direct Three.js prototype into a typed, tested game through short implementation rounds: isolate one problem, change the smallest owner, prove it in the browser, record the result, and land it on main.

title: Start with hard constraints
text: The project is browser-native and built directly on Three.js rather than a general game engine. The simulation runs at a fixed 60 Hz, playable tanks use first-party procedural runtime geometry, and presentation pages stay isolated from the heavy game boot graph. Those constraints shaped the architecture: deterministic rules can run in Node, the renderer adapts independently, and every public claim can point to code, a test, a capture, or a measured receipt.

title: Separate rules from presentation
text: Movement, ballistics, armor, damage, spotting, match state, and bot decisions live behind renderer-free contracts. Three.js turns the latest state into cameras, rigs, lighting, effects, audio, and UI without becoming the authority for a hit. That boundary lets local battles and browser-hosted rooms share the same combat rules. It also lets lower-end visual settings reduce cost without changing gameplay.

title: Claude Code and Codex workflow
text: Claude Code and Codex were used as development tools across bounded tasks. Broad or risky work moved into isolated Git worktrees; each lane named the files it owned, preserved unrelated changes, and exchanged exact commit hashes and evidence before integration. The working rule was simple: main stays current, unfinished experiments stay isolated, and a branch is not proof. Only the integrated bytes count. Human direction set the target and acceptance bar; agents implemented, measured, reviewed, and documented against it.

title: Build, falsify, and measure
text: A typical round starts with a reproducible baseline, then attribution. The smallest plausible fix is tested with focused self-tests, browser interaction, console inspection, screenshots, and performance probes. A result must survive a second run or a deliberately hostile case before it is accepted. Visual work is judged from current pixels, not only numeric checks. Performance work records cold and warm conditions, device constraints, long tasks, frame gaps, GPU resources, and transition timings instead of reporting a single FPS number.

title: Make the workflow durable
text: Repository-level AGENTS.md, indexed subsystem SKILL.md files, and one maintained architecture decision record preserve ownership, invariants, required commands, and recurring failure modes without burying contributors in completed migration notes. When a manual process repeats, it becomes a script or a gate. That is why model screenshots, combat anatomy, vehicle icons, route probes, public metadata, and release checks are reproducible from the repository. Raw execution receipts stay in Git history or ignored QA artifacts.

title: Land only integrated proof
text: A finished change is committed as one coherent unit, rebased on the latest origin/main, and rechecked after integration. The final push verifies that its parent is still the remote tip so concurrent work cannot silently overwrite a newer landing. The public build then proves route isolation and strips non-distributable comparison material. This keeps the playable site, source tree, documentation, and main branch describing the same game.

title: From reference to playable machine
text: Kevin B. Liu authored every playable tank as first-party procedural runtime geometry. References guide proportion and detail, but the shipped machine is rebuilt from code, connected to combat data, rendered into its own icon set, and released through measured and visual gates.

title: Research and reference intake
text: A model round begins with source photographs, published dimensions, plan and side references, or a comparison mesh when its license permits authoring use. The source is an oracle for recognizable shape—not a playable asset and not an automatic truth when the reference itself is wrong. Proportion comes first: hull length and width, turret station, roof height, gun length, wheel count, track course, and major armor masses must read correctly before small fittings are added.

title: Build the visible machine from parts
text: Procedural builders assemble hull plates, turret shells, mantlets, barrels, running gear, optics, hatches, smoke launchers, baskets, antennas, armor kits, and stowage from reusable geometry and material vocabulary. Station-section measurements keep front, middle, and rear masses faithful instead of stretching one generic box. Camouflage-aware structural parts and neutral mechanical parts use explicit roles. Comparison GLBs never become a hidden production fallback.

title: Rig articulation and running gear
text: Hull, turret, gun mount, recoil group, muzzle, wheels, return rollers, sprockets, idlers, and linked tracks have explicit owners. Turret equipment must rotate with the turret and remain visibly seated; hull equipment must not follow it. The muzzle bore must be open and resolve from the actual barrel hierarchy. Suspension samples terrain at each support station. Native running gear preserves the correct wheel count and track path while avoiding duplicated donor wheels, clipping shoes, or floating attachments.

title: Author combat anatomy from the same shape
text: Armor plates, spaced layers, ERA, modules, ammunition, fuel, crew, and articulation anchors are calibrated to the checked vehicle frame. The game therefore uses the same authored shape for presentation, impact tracing, internal damage, and the technical side diagrams. Structural cupolas can participate in hit geometry. Sights, machine guns, baskets, antennas, and loose equipment remain presentation fittings unless gameplay explicitly gives them a physical role.

title: Generate icons and technical cards
text: The asset pipeline renders the current procedural rig into garage and gallery imagery, transparent silhouettes, armor diagrams, separate module and crew diagrams, tier treatments, and supporting presentation views. One deterministic angle capture now emits both portrait sizes through a shared framing policy, so a new tank cannot leave behind a hand-cropped or stale thumbnail. Use npm run tank:portraits -- --ids=<changed ids> and npm run tank:portraits:check -- --ids=<changed ids> for portrait-only work. The complete release sequence remains npm run tank:anatomy:update, npm run tank:anatomy:check, then npm run tank:release:check -- --ids=<changed ids> --gate.

title: Measure, inspect, and graduate
text: Automated gates check geometry fingerprints, dimensions, stations, floaters, track intersections, wheel quality, muzzle bores, materials, armor anatomy, markings, provenance, and deterministic asset freshness. Standard front, quarter, side, rear, top, close, and yaw views then expose defects a numeric score can miss. A model graduates only when every required view clears the visual acceptance floor, attachments have physical load paths, winding and backfaces are healthy, and the clean integrated release check passes. The Tank Gallery is the live inspection surface for that final procedural rig.

title: Every hit has a path
text: The battle simulation advances at 60 Hz. Movement, aim, ballistics, armor, damage, reloads, spotting, and match results are resolved from authoritative state—not from the rendered frame.

title: Fixed-step battle loop
text: The authoritative step uses metres, seconds, radians, and a fixed 1/60-second interval. Input is sampled into explicit vehicle controls before movement, combat, spotting, and result evaluation run in a stable order. Render rate can change without changing the number or order of simulation steps. Frame-time spikes accumulate into bounded fixed steps. Authoritative randomness is seeded or injected. Wall-clock time and Math.random() are excluded from rules that affect a shot, reload, module state, or match result.

title: Aim and shot creation
text: Camera aim and gun aim are separate. The camera chooses the requested point; traverse, elevation, suspension attitude, and bore obstruction determine where the barrel can actually point. A shot starts at the resolved muzzle transform with the current shell, velocity, dispersion, and owner identity. The HUD draws both states. The camera marker communicates the request. The gun marker communicates the ballistic line. “Path blocked” and gun-limit feedback therefore describe physical constraints instead of repainting the request as truth.

title: Armor trace and penetration
text: The shell segment is tested against world collision before vehicle armor. Vehicle queries transform the ray into the target pose, order plate crossings, calculate distance and angle, apply normalization or ricochet rules, and consume the shell’s remaining penetration. Spaced layers and internal volumes stay in traversal order. A penetration continues through internal module and crew volumes. A non-penetration still produces an authoritative impact event. Presentation receives the resolved path and result; it does not rerun the decision.

title: Damage, reloads, and special weapons
text: Damage updates hit points, tracks, engine, fuel, ammunition, gun, turret drive, optics, and crew state. Autoloaders distinguish intra-clip delay from magazine reload. Guided missiles retain a live projectile and steering state until impact or expiry. Fires, ammunition-rack events, ramming, and repairs use the same event boundary. The X-ray replay, hit card, damage log, reload rack, impact effects, and sound all consume those events. This keeps visible feedback aligned with the result used by solo and multiplayer authority.

title: Battle rules
text: Standard Battle, Capture the Flag, Zone Control, Turbo Ball, and Endless Horde compose over the same complete tank simulation. Flag and zone modes add six-second respawns. Turbo Ball keeps weapons active while tanks drive at 1.85× mobility and shells can strike the ball. Horde escalates deterministic waves of fragile bots and places repair caches. The renderer-free mode controller owns scores, objectives, respawn timers, wave state, caches, and bot objective points. Solo, private rooms, and LAN rooms use the same rules; the host choice travels in canonical lobby state and survives rematches.

title: Bosses, infection, critical damage and weapon ladders
text: Juggernaut lets you play the boss or join the hunters. The boss is 12% larger, has a pulsing shield aura, eight times its hull health and half its reload time. Hunters respawn; the boss must survive ten minutes. Infected starts with five infected (at least three in custom battles). Survivors have 130% health; infected have 20%, 30% more speed and their own reload, and hunt the survivors as a pack, returning five seconds after every death. Destroyed survivors join the infected. Survive three minutes, or convert everyone. Both modes play with unlimited rounds. Realistic uses normal spotting and removes hull HP attrition. Penetrations reliably injure crew, apply 2.5× module damage and spread fragments through the struck compartments. Fires damage modules four times faster. Ammunition destruction, fewer than two crew or a destroyed engine and gun eliminate the tank. Gun Game advances through five weapons with two kills per stage; respawns preserve progress.

title: Direct drone flight and the AC-130 scope
text: In Drone mode, press V or tap the drone control to launch a quadcopter from your tank. After the launch animation you directly pilot its first-person view. W/S move, A/D strafe, Space climbs and mouse or touch look steers; pitch down and fly forward to dive. The battery lasts 40 seconds within an 850 m radius. Fly into an enemy to deliver an explosive impact. Once you are flying its feed, V returns you to your parked, vulnerable tank: the drone flies home, lands on its dock and is ready again 5 seconds after landing; after an impact, an empty battery or a lost link the next drone takes 25 seconds. V does nothing during the launch. National drones have detailed service airframes, camera gimbals and payloads. Large turrets carry the launch rail; compact turrets may use the hull. Impact, battery expiry and a lost link trigger a short static transition; a return closes the feed cleanly. The minimap tracks the drone separately from its carrier. I or the sensor button cycles white-hot infrared, colored thermal, green night vision and daylight; the same options are available in tank scopes. Heat highlights visible tanks and bright explosions, without bypassing cover or spotting. The AC-130 follows an automatic orbit with an overhead aiming scope. Mouse or touch controls aim; the wheel zooms. Select the 30 mm autocannon, 152 mm explosive howitzer or guided missiles with 1–3 or the ammunition buttons. These have independent reload channels and unlimited ammunition. Shots and drone impacts use the same host-authoritative collision, armor and damage rules as tank weapons. Protect the vulnerable allied ground convoy: escorts have 90% hull strength and must physically reach the green E extraction marker. Save at least half before the eight-minute deadline; losing too many allies fails the mission. The objective tracks surviving troops, rescued troops and route progress. In multiplayer every pilot supplies air support while separate allied bots drive the convoy. Enemies cannot see or shoot the aircraft. Howitzer blasts reach 22 m and missile blasts reach 18 m. J drops ammunition and K drops medical supplies at the ground aim point; icons support touch input. Crates land after six seconds. Nearby allies that need them detour to collect them. Ammo restores finite ground reserves; medicine repairs 35% of maximum health. Cooldowns are 22/30 seconds and crates expire after 70 seconds. The minimap shows the aircraft, orbit, ground aim, extraction and supplies.

title: Verification
text: Node-runnable self-tests cover movement, combat, spotting, missile guidance, special actions, AI aim, and the complete authoritative match. Browser probes add bore parity, projectile travel, live impact effects, and HUD alignment. Run node src/sim/combat.selftest.mjs, node src/sim/authoritativeMatch.selftest.mjs, and npm test after changing shared combat rules.

title: Standard Battle and team setup
text: Standard Battle is elimination: defeat the opposing team before the fifteen-minute clock ends. Destroyed vehicles do not respawn. The scoreboard carries the essential information, so this mode has no extra objective banner. Choose 7 v 7, 14 v 14 or custom teams before launch. In custom solo battles, the player counts as an ally; the field limit is 42 vehicles and allied bots yield when needed to preserve the requested enemy count. Battle Setup stores settings for each mode. Team presets, enemy nation and eligible times of day are chosen before starting. The Battle button launches the configured game; Multiplayer has its own entry for creating or joining a room without accidentally starting a solo match.

title: Capture the Flag
text: Take the enemy flag back to your own base while protecting your home flag. The default target is three captures, with a fifteen-minute clock and six-second respawns; setup can change the score and respawn settings. A flag carrier keeps its full speed. Recovering a dropped friendly flag and escorting a carrier can be more valuable than chasing a distant kill. Use fast vehicles for the run, keep a defender near home and cover the carrier’s return lane. Bots assign carrier, recovery, escort, raid and defense roles rather than sending the entire team to one flag. Destroying an enemy opens a route, but a kill is not a flag capture.

title: Zone Control and Gravity Mode
text: Zone Control rewards taking and holding three sectors. The default target is 750 points, with six-second respawns and a fifteen-minute clock. Destroying an opposing tank adds 25 points in Zone Control and Gravity Mode. Spread pressure across the map: leaving every sector to pursue one damaged tank gives the enemy time to score. Gravity Mode uses the zone objective with a twelve-minute clock, rocket jumps, boosted mobility and selectable gravity. Mars is 0.38 g, Moon 0.17 g and Earth 1 g. Cache frequency is configurable. Its default vehicle modifiers are 1.25× speed, 1.2× hull health, 0.9× damage and 0.9× reload time. Recoil and airborne motion matter: choose a landing zone before launching.

title: Turbo Ball
text: Drive or shoot the ball into the enemy goal. The default match lasts ten minutes, ends at five goals and uses three-second respawns. Vehicles have 0.6 g gravity, 1.85× speed, 1.5× hull health, half damage and 0.7× reload time. Ammunition is unlimited; equipment, consumables and critical module damage are disabled for this mode. Get behind the ball, line up the goal and commit to a controlled push. Jumping and amplified recoil enable aerial plays but can overshoot the ball. A striker, supporting screens and a goal defender make a stronger team than several tanks wedged around the same contact point. Destroying tanks disrupts the opposition; goals decide the score.

title: Endless Horde and Frontline Assault
text: Endless Horde has no match clock or respawns, and rounds are unlimited. Your side has twice its hull health; attackers arrive at 15% of theirs, 2% tougher each wave. Survive waves that grow from six attackers by two each wave, with an additional surge every third wave under the default settings. Clearing a wave repairs 30% of maximum hull health; use the floating repair caches to sustain the run. Setup can change the allied support, hostile identity pool, opening wave and enemy nation. Frontline Assault is a sequential breakthrough: take three sectors against escalating defenders, then hold the final sector for twenty seconds. The default clock is twelve minutes and running out of time is a defeat. Campaign operations vary the battlefield and difficulty; clearing an operation opens the next. Preserve your hull for the final hold rather than treating it like a respawn mode.

title: Driving, airtime and landing damage
text: Movement runs at a fixed sixty steps per second. Engine power, weight, forward and reverse limits, track condition, terrain resistance and hull rotation jointly determine handling. The renderer interpolates those states rather than changing movement with frame rate. Handbrake behavior is grounded; landing after a jump must not silently latch the brake. A fall is a physical impact, not just a height threshold. Mass, impact speed, attitude and mode physics affect the result. Reduced gravity changes both your arc and the terrain you can safely reach. Avoid blind drops at bridge abutments or cliff edges; use a route with a visible landing and enough room to settle.

title: The model moves as one machine
text: Every selectable tank is a first-party procedural runtime rig. The same vehicle record drives its geometry, dimensions, armor, internal anatomy, mobility, gun, ammunition, icon set, garage dossier, and battle behavior.

title: Vehicle contract
text: A vehicle spec defines identity, class, nation, tier, dimensions, mass, engine output, speed, traverse, gun limits, shells, armor, modules, crew, equipment policy, and builder. Consumers read the registry instead of carrying parallel facts. Entity IDs are not vehicle spec IDs. Multiplayer permits duplicate tank selections, so identity, ownership, and specification remain separate throughout state and presentation.

title: Procedural rig
text: Builders create hull, turret, gun mount, gun, running gear, tracks, optics, fittings, markings, and damage hooks with stable ownership. Tank forward is local +Z. Articulation occurs at explicit pivots, and the muzzle is resolved from the actual barrel hierarchy. Roof equipment can move with the turret without becoming armor. Cupolas participate in hit geometry; machine guns, antennas, baskets, loose stowage, and presentation-only fittings do not.

title: Suspension and tracks
text: Each supported wheel samples terrain beneath its own station. The visual suspension settles to those contacts, the hull derives pitch and roll from support, and the track path is rebuilt around the moved wheels. Swedish siege suspension adds commanded hull attitude without breaking gun tracking. Track animation follows traveled distance and side speed. Damage can detach a side, remove its running band, throw a persistent ribbon, and leave loose running-gear pieces.

title: Combat anatomy
text: Armor plates, modules, and crew stations are authored in the vehicle frame and transformed with the live pose. Generated side diagrams are receipts for that same data. They are not separately drawn approximations. Any playable geometry or profile change runs tank:anatomy:update, tank:anatomy:check, then the targeted gated release check. This refreshes armor, module, crew, icon, and technical-diagram evidence together.

title: Fleet release gate
text: Appearance, bore, material, wheel, recoil, combat anatomy, provenance, and profile-specific checks run before a vehicle is considered current. Playable loading never falls back to a comparison GLB. The Tank Gallery constructs the live builder and overlays the canonical diagnostic volumes, which makes it the fastest manual review surface for a vehicle change.

title: Choose a role, then a vehicle
text: Light tanks and reconnaissance IFVs trade protection for scouting, repositioning and support. The Sheridan family leads the fleet in base view range. A high view range does not reveal every enemy: camouflage, cover, smoke and line of sight still determine detection. Main battle tanks combine armor, gun handling and mobility in different proportions; a heavy front plate does not protect the sides, roof or internal modules. Use the searchable fleet reference below to compare base hull and turret rotation, dispersion, aim time, reload, speed, view range and supported systems. These are game balance values, not claims about classified real-world performance. Garage figures include your fitted equipment; mode bonuses and combat damage can change the resulting battle performance.

title: Vehicle systems and their controls
text: The compact console above ammunition only offers systems that the selected vehicle or mode supports. E selects or toggles an ATGM, G launches smoke, N toggles lights, B toggles a remote automatic gun, and F jumps in jump-enabled modes. The displayed key hints are the immediate reference. A reload countdown replaces the weapon label while that system is unavailable. Smoke grenades leave the authored launcher sockets, fly forward in an arc and develop into expanding, drifting clouds. They interrupt spotting and targeting through the cloud, providing space to withdraw or cross an exposed lane. Smoke does not stop shells already in flight. Remote guns need a suitable visible target and a clear firing path; they animate independently of the main cannon. Hydropneumatic aiming is only available on vehicles equipped for it.

title: Equipment, ammunition and technical diagrams
text: Equipment benefits appear directly in the final garage values rather than as an old-to-new comparison. Compare turret traverse and dispersion as well as reload, mobility and vision: a handling improvement can matter more than raw damage. Each shell has its own penetration, velocity, damage and ammunition count. Guided racks and conventional cannon ammunition may use different reload channels. Open the information controls or Tank Gallery for vehicle-specific armor, module and crew diagrams generated from the actual first-party model. They explain why a hit can disable a track, damage an engine or injure crew without destroying the hull. The current vehicle geometry and calibration receipts, rather than one generic tank drawing, supply these diagrams.

title: Rendering can adapt without changing the rules
text: Three.js owns presentation only. Adaptive resolution, shadows, vegetation, post-processing, particles, and warmup can change with the device; the 60 Hz battle model remains unchanged.

title: Frame composition
text: The render path updates camera, visible vehicle rigs, world detail, presentation effects, lighting, shadows, and post-processing from the latest interpolated state. Established hot loops reuse scratch objects and pools rather than allocating each frame. Late transparent effects share depth information with the main scene. Muzzle light, tracer, sparks, smoke, dust, fire, and debris are admitted by distance and quality policy.

title: Lighting and post-processing
text: Biome lighting supplies sun direction, sky, fog, exposure, and shadow policy. Stable cascaded shadows follow the relevant camera region. The post chain combines ambient occlusion, anti-aliasing, bloom where useful, output grading, and the final dynamic render scale. Capture views pin quality and render scale so comparison images do not drift. Gameplay can reduce expensive layers under sustained load.

title: Adaptive quality
text: Desktop and mobile resolve separate starting profiles. Internal resolution, shadow work, vegetation density, effect budgets, and post features can step down independently. Hysteresis prevents rapid oscillation. Device diagnostics and measured overload—not user-agent labels alone—select the safe path. A quality change never alters shell travel, spotting, damage, or authoritative timing.

title: Loading and recovery
text: Boot-critical modules avoid importing the complete fleet builder graph. Deferred vehicle construction, shader warmup, offscreen preparation, and cached garage residents flatten transition spikes. Context-loss handling restores presentation state without inventing battle state. Screenshot and loading probes treat black frames, stale swaps, console errors, and incomplete garage models as failures.

title: Performance evidence
text: Performance traces record frame categories, renderer counters, dynamic scale, and transition budgets. Browser probes cover cold load, battle entry, map switching, the garage, and multiplayer rendering. Use npm run perf:dev, npm run perf:cold, npm run perf:transitions, and a production build for renderer work.

title: Headlights, shadows and smoke
text: Driving lights use actual model apertures and follow the hull’s pose. Their warm beams now illuminate farther ahead; only the nearest eligible sources occupy a fixed light pool, while the other visible lamp lenses may still glow. Switching lights off or destroying a tank removes its contribution. Periscopes, mirrors and unrelated armor must not glow just because they share a material. Ambient occlusion and cast shadows are separate. Turning AO off should not remove sun shadows. Shadow stability, cloud history and effects composition have dedicated checks for moving cameras, firing and quality changes. Smoke is both a rendered volume effect and a simulation visibility blocker; the picture and the spotting decision have separate owners that must agree.

title: Measure the frame that the player actually feels
text: Performance work covers cold boot, garage residency, battle acquisition, countdown warmup, the first ten seconds of combat, steady-state frame pacing, device adaptation, and recovery—not just an average frame-rate number.

title: Keep boot and routes isolated
text: The garage does not build a battlefield until concrete Battle intent. Public pages do not import the playable renderer, and garage boot does not eagerly import the complete simulation or fleet graph. Exact vehicle-family and world work is acquired only when the selected route needs it. Cold-load probes disable caches and record network plus application work so a warm navigation cannot masquerade as first-visit performance.

title: Stage battle loading behind cover
text: Battle entry acquires the exact world and roster, uploads required textures, prepares effects, submits vehicle materials, warms shaders and post-processing, and establishes the first valid camera before reveal. Required work finishes before the countdown instead of surfacing as a black or frozen opening frame. Progress reflects owned stages. Stale work is cancelled when intent changes, and a retryable lifecycle owns recovery rather than scattering timers through the composition root.

title: Record full frame evidence
text: The development flight recorder stores route transitions, long tasks, frame gaps, renderer counters, resolution, simulation debt, memory, and named spans. The performance HUD exposes live statistics for focused probes and saves event histories for later attribution. Opening-battle probes focus on the first ten seconds after the countdown because shader births, roster commits, audio startup, and effect bursts often hide there.

title: Reduce work at its owner
text: Static garage presentation sleeps between invalidations. Established frame loops reuse scratch objects, rank or stagger expensive updates, pool transient effects, cache stable worlds, demand-load vehicle families, and remove invisible render submissions rather than merely lowering visual quality. Optimization is accepted only when the same scenario improves without shifting cost into loading, memory, correctness, or a later frame.

title: Adapt to the real device
text: Capability probes and measured overload choose render scale, shadows, vegetation, effect budgets, and post-processing. Desktop, mobile, and constrained profiles start differently, then adjust with hysteresis to avoid visible oscillation. GPU recovery validates framebuffers and can step down optional presentation layers. Simulation frequency, ballistics, armor, and network authority remain unchanged.

title: Budgets and release evidence
text: Release probes cover cold load, transitions, battle opening, sustained play, map and tank switching, returned garage state, mobile layouts, and constrained CPU/network profiles. Reports include p95 frame gaps, long tasks, program births, draw work, memory, and readiness time. Use npm run perf:cold, npm run perf:dev, npm run perf:resources:gate, npm run qa:device, and npm run build for the corresponding performance claims.

title: Graphics recovery and stale sessions
text: The browser may reclaim a graphics context under memory pressure. The game pauses presentation and restores resources behind cover before resuming. Quality recovery should be bounded, preserve the battle state and avoid repeated allocation. A reload is the fallback when restoration cannot complete; it is not the normal way to switch maps or vehicles. When a regular tab behaves differently from a fresh tab, compare the served application version and saved graphics settings before attributing it to one render effect. Hashed assets and deployment-version checks protect against mixed releases. Record the map, vehicle, quality, viewport and reproduction steps with a report; a screenshot alone cannot establish whether the cause is stale assets, settings or GPU state.

title: Battlefields are built for armored movement
text: Thirty-three battlefields offer distinct routes, settlements, elevation, cover and skies. Learn how map selection works, explore the current atlas and understand what terrain means for movement and tactics.

title: Map contract
text: Each map provides terrain height, ground materials, obstacles, collision, concealment, spawn groups, capture areas, lighting, weather, sound context, and a deterministic establishing camera. Simulation consumers use these interfaces rather than scene traversal. The registry is the source for selection, loading, Studio, screenshots, and documentation counts.

title: Terrain and movement
text: Height fields answer vehicle support, projectile collision, camera clearance, and prop placement. Surface class affects grip and presentation. Roads, slopes, ridges, water edges, and hull-down positions are composed around the intended armored routes. Vehicle suspension samples the same ground surface used by movement and ballistic terrain queries.

title: Structures and utilities
text: Structure families expose readable openings, material sets, damage states, and collision. Utility networks connect poles and lines across valid spans. Large cover blocks sightlines; small visual fittings do not become invisible walls. Detached doors, barriers, street pieces, and other loose props enter bounded physics with stable sleep and cleanup rules.

title: Destruction and wrecks
text: Destroyed vehicles retain wreck geometry, detached tracks, fire, smoke, and debris. Map wrecks and disassembled garage pieces use modern first-party vehicle families. Turrets, hulls, wheels, ERA, and weapons remain decoration unless explicitly registered for collision. Persistent aftermath is presentation state derived from authoritative destruction events.

title: Map quality gates
text: Automated checks audit spawns, bounds, material coverage, structures, utilities, collision, wrecks, loose props, and placement. Deterministic battle captures expose bad silhouettes and obstructed routes that numeric gates cannot. Run node src/world/mapQuality.selftest.mjs, the nearby world self-tests, and targeted screenshot views after map changes.

title: Picking maps and times of day
text: The current catalog contains 33 battlefields. Pick a specific map or use Random. Ordinary random selection excludes the dedicated Mars and Moon battlefields, and consecutive solo draws avoid the previous map. Multiplayer uses the host’s selected battlefield so every peer shares the same world. The full atlas below uses the approved current map pictures. Day, sunset and night are weighted 60:30:10 when all are enabled. Disabling a time redistributes those weights over the remaining choices; at least one must remain enabled. Earthrise Basin places a large Earth in its lunar sky. Aegis Crossing is a lush green cliff-and-bridge battlefield with buildings around the crossing. Read routes and elevation as well as the thumbnail: a spectacular drop can still be fatal.

title: One bot controller for every battlefield
text: Solo and authoritative multiplayer bots use the same renderer-free decision logic. They navigate a seeded battlefield graph, respect team and visibility rules, choose viable shots, use vehicle capabilities, and remain testable without a GPU.

title: Perception and target choice
text: Bots consume the same team, visibility, range, health, and vehicle-state contracts used by authority. They do not read rendered objects or hidden client-only coordinates. Candidate targets are scored from current tactical state rather than selected by scene proximity alone. Difficulty changes reaction, aim quality, engagement distance, and decision pressure without granting information the bot should not have.

title: Seeded route planning
text: One typed traversability grid is built per match from terrain mobility, world collision, openings, objectives, and vehicle capabilities. The planner supplies deterministic paths around blocked cells while local steering handles immediate alignment and avoidance. Route decisions can be reproduced in Node across every map, including heavy vehicles, tracked damage, steep slopes, and objective modes.

title: Gun handling and fire control
text: The controller respects turret traverse, elevation and depression, bore obstruction, reloads, magazines, dispersion, shell velocity, penetration, and target motion. It aims for hittable armor and internal weak areas when the current weapon and angle make that shot credible. Autocannons, single-shot guns, autoloaders, and guided weapons share the same decision boundary but apply their own cadence and ammunition state.

title: Team safety and pressure
text: Friendly vehicles are rejected from valid shot paths, and the controller avoids firing through allies. Bots spread their attention, move to useful lanes, support objectives, and keep enough separation to avoid turning one friendly cluster into an obstacle. Enemy bots and allied bots use the same logic. Team assignment changes targets and objectives, not competence.

title: Survival and recovery
text: Bots consider exposure, cover, damaged tracks, disabled modules, repair opportunities, ammo state, and nearby threats. They can disengage from a losing angle, recover movement, re-path after destruction, and continue contributing instead of waiting in open ground. Mode objectives layer onto these survival decisions so capture, defense, escort, and horde pressure do not require separate fake movement systems.

title: Verification
text: Focused AI tests cover aim, friendly-fire rejection, routes, difficulty, deterministic decisions, and authoritative bot integration. Map-wide server tests run the controller without rendering, while browser battles verify that visible movement, firing, and effects match those decisions. Bot changes run node src/game/ai.selftest.mjs, node src/sim/ai.aim.selftest.mjs, node src/sim/botRoutePlanner.selftest.mjs, and node server/authoritativeBots.selftest.mjs.

title: Classic, Jev and coordinated objectives
text: Classic and Jev share the local driving, aiming, visibility and vehicle-system logic on both allied and enemy teams. Jev adds bounded team-level orders; it does not bypass spotting or replace the physical driver. Choose the brain and difficulty before the next match. An allied team should not retain an older behavior set just because it fights alongside the player. Flag teams distribute recovery, escort and raiding roles. Turbo Ball retains a striker long enough to circle behind the ball and line up a push, with screening and defensive support. Zone teams distribute capture pressure. Mobile units can flank while anchors maintain pressure; navigation includes right-of-way for the human, committed passing and safe reversing when vehicles block one another.

title: Smoke, remote guns and safe jumps
text: Bots can deploy fitted smoke when withdrawing, under pressure or reloading, and operate remote automatic guns against eligible visible opponents. They only request a jump when the mode allows it and the prospective landing is affordable. Cliff and bridge approaches need a valid route; a direct line to the objective is not enough. Behavior tests include all 33 maps, flag and ball scenarios, congestion, fall-risk decisions and a large Jev team workload. Their guarantees are scoped to the tested scenarios: they catch regressions in decisions and bounded work, but do not prove that a bot will solve every possible terrain or traffic situation.

title: Play together
text: Start a room, send the code, and fight beside your friends or against them.

title: Start a room
text: Open Multiplayer and pick one of three ways in. Private room Create a room and send its six-character code or invite link to your friends. Enter a room code Type the code from your host, or open their invite link. Local network One computer runs npm run server:mp (port 8792); everyone on the same network picks Local network and plays through it.

title: Seats
text: Two sides and a gallery. The room sets its team size; empty seats can fill with bots. Team Alpha v Team Bravo Spectator 7 a side by default up to 14 a side A room holds up to 28 players and 8 spectators. New players join the smaller side; the room's creator can lock team switching. Empty seats fill with bots unless the room turns that off. Everyone brings their own tank, camouflage and up to 3 equipment items; two players can pick the same tank. Names are up to 24 characters; a name already taken gets a number.

title: Modes
text: A room plays any battle mode; the Proving Ground stays solo. Standard Battle Capture the Flag Zone Control Turbo Ball Endless Horde Frontline Assault Gravity Mode Juggernaut Infected Realistic Gun Game Drone AC-130 In Endless Horde and Frontline Assault, everyone deploys on one side, up to 7 players, against the waves.

title: Ready up
text: 1 Pick your tank, camouflage and equipment, then press Ready. 2 The room's creator starts the battle once every connected player is ready. 3 The creator's browser hosts the battle; on a local network, the helper does.

title: Leaving and rejoining
text: Drop out and your seat waits 5 minutes; open the link again to take it back. If the host's browser goes away, the room hands the battle to another player within 8 s and play goes on. If the creator leaves, the room's settings pass to the longest-seated player after 30 s. A room closes 24 hours after its last message. Room chat keeps the last 48 messages, up to 240 characters each.

title: Fair play
text: The host decides every hit, reload and result; the others send only their controls. You receive only the enemies your team has spotted: a hidden tank's position never reaches your browser.

title: Hear the battle the way a crew does
text: What every shot, warning and engine tells you, and how to set the mix.

title: Did it go in?
text: No interface sound tells you a shot hit: you hear it at the target, late by the distance, and about half a second later your gunner calls it. Your crew says It means Penetration. Target. Through the armor. The round went through. No penetration. Didn't go through. It hit but did not go through: aim for thinner armour. Ricochet. Bounced. It glanced off an angled plate. Miss. Short. Adjusting. Nothing hit: correct your aim. Good hit. Something's damaged. Critical hit. It went in and broke a module. Ammo rack hit. He's cooking off. His ammunition is burning: he is about to blow. Hit his engine. His engine is hit: he slows down or catches fire. His track's off. He's immobilized. His track is off: he cannot move until he repairs it. Their crew's hit. One of his crew is down. Target destroyed. Target down. Tank knocked out. Your shot finished him. How late you hear it Earth 100 m: 0.3 s 500 m: 1.5 s 1000 m: 2.9 s Mars 100 m: 0.4 s 500 m: 2.1 s 1000 m: 4.0 s

title: Crew warnings
text: When something happens to your tank, the crew says so before you see it. Your crew says It means We're hit. Taking hits. A shot went into your tank. Armor held. It bounced. A shot hit you and did no harm. Fire! Engine compartment! Fire in the hull! You are burning: put it out or keep losing hull. Ammo rack hit! Ammunition damaged! Your ammunition is damaged: the reload slows. Engine's damaged. Engine hit. Losing power. Your engine is hit: less power, and it may catch fire. Track's gone. We're immobilized. Lost a track. A track is off: you cannot move until it is fixed. Main gun's damaged. Gun's hit. Your main gun is damaged until it is repaired. Armor's failing. Can't take much more. Little hull is left: get to cover. We're spotted. They have eyes on us. An enemy has spotted you; the sixth-sense lamp lights too. Missile incoming! Incoming missile, brace! A guided missile is on its way: move or break its line of sight. Drone inbound! Drone on us, overhead! An enemy drone is overhead.

title: Crew radio
text: Each nation's crew speaks its own language: 13 crews in all. American English British English German Russian Ukrainian Chinese French Swedish Japanese Korean Italian Polish Hebrew One call plays at a time; survival warnings cut in front. A damaged radio narrows the voice, adds static and drops words. Settings › Sound › Crew voices: National crews follow each tank's nation, or pick one of the 13 existing national crews for every tank; the choice is saved across battles and reloads.

title: Gunfire
text: Every weapon fires one of 18 report classes; the bigger the gun, the louder and longer its report. Rifle-calibre machine gun 118 dB Heavy machine gun 124 dB 20 mm autocannon 128 dB 25 mm autocannon 130 dB 30 mm autocannon 132 dB Anti-tank missile 132 dB AC-130 autocannon 134 dB 40 mm autocannon 135 dB AC-130 missile 136 dB 50 mm autocannon 137 dB 90 mm gun 141 dB 105 mm gun 144 dB Heavy rocket 145 dB 120 mm gun 147 dB 125 mm gun 148 dB 130 mm gun 150 dB AC-130 howitzer 150 dB 152 mm gun 152 dB A distant shot is seen before it is heard, and hills between you and it muffle it. On Mars sound travels at 240 m/s and arrives 14 dB quieter and thinner. On the Moon almost nothing carries (60 dB less): you hear your own tank through its hull. In the sight your own gun sounds from inside the turret, and the world outside dulls.

title: Engines and tracks
text: Each hull carries its own powertrain's sound: gas turbines spool and whine, diesels shift and rumble. Tracks change with the ground and your speed: earth, hard surface, mud, sand, snow and water. An enemy drone buzzes where it flies and rises in pitch as it closes.

title: Sound settings
text: Settings › Sound has six sliders and two alarms; changes apply at once. Master volume Engine & mechanical volume Gunfire & impacts volume Ambience volume (wind, birds, garage) Interface & music volume Crew voices & alarms volume Critical-damage heartbeat pulse Concussion muffle and ear ringing after close blasts Every sound is a recording made for Claude of Tanks with ElevenLabs before release; nothing is generated while you play.

title: Read the tank without losing the view
text: The garage, HUD, sight, killcam, spectator mode, after-action report, settings, keyboard, pointer, controller, and touch input share one control and typography system.

title: Garage and deployment
text: The garage combines vehicle selection, dossier, ammunition, equipment, camouflage, map choice, match mode, room state, and launch. Selection and displayed pedestal identity remain synchronized through explicit state. The interface links directly to Tank Gallery for deeper geometry inspection and to Scene Studio for composition work.

title: Battle HUD
text: The HUD prioritizes score, time, teams, reticle state, ammunition, consumables, minimap, damage, spotting, and short event feedback. It does not restate every system continuously. Reload racks use the authoritative magazine state. Damage panels use current modules. Team and minimap information obey the spotting boundary.

title: Death, killcam, and spectating
text: A death beat shows the player’s destruction before the X-ray replay. If the battle continues, the camera moves to a living ally. The compact switcher identifies the vehicle, its position in the living roster, equal previous and next controls, and a quiet garage exit. Mouse movement orbits the ally without turning a turret. Keyboard and touch targets retain a minimum 44-pixel interaction size.

title: Input and mobile
text: Keyboard, mouse, pointer-lock fallback, free look, zoom, touch joysticks, swipe aim, pinch scope, shell selection, special actions, and consumables normalize into game input. UI ownership prevents a text field or dialog from leaking keys into battle. Safe-area layout, compact labels, and device-specific quality preserve the same battle rules on phones. Settings → Gameplay → Edit HUD layout lets you drag or hide panels over a battlefield preview, with separate desktop, portrait, and landscape layouts. Save applies changes; Cancel discards them; Reset restores responsive defaults.

title: Accessibility and regression checks
text: Semantic buttons, visible focus, reduced-motion handling, descriptive media alternatives, contrast, and touch sizing are part of the public and in-game surfaces. Responsive QA covers desktop and 390-pixel layouts. Minimal battle HUD keeps the aiming reticle, range, zoom, ammunition/reload, and scope vision controls while hiding other battle panels. Touch driving and firing remain available. F10 toggles the display, Esc opens Settings, and a three-finger tap restores the full HUD. Focused tests cover keyboard ownership, settings, layout editing and persistence, icons, flags, loading screens, spectator controls, and touch controls.

title: A compact garage and readable battle HUD
text: Open Choose how you play to configure each mode, then use Battle to launch. The separate hexagonal Multiplayer control opens room setup. Map cards show compact biome tags; hover reveals the magnifier, and selecting an already selected map opens its larger preview. Camouflage names occupy one line, with compact collection and nation filters above the scrollable swatches. Hold Tab to expand the team lists. Lists remain readable through 14 vehicles per side; larger teams use an icon grid. The penetration panel simplifies its numeric detail for large rosters so the vehicle diagrams remain contained and visible. Scope magnification sits with the central aiming information. Objective, detection and team notifications occupy separate reserved areas; Standard Battle omits the extra objective strip.

title: Settings, clean captures and phone orientation
text: Settings separates gameplay, sound, graphics and language. Choose AI difficulty and Classic or Jev behavior for the next battle. The UI-free setting hides gameplay overlays for unobstructed viewing; restore it through Settings when you need the HUD again. It is a viewing control, not a replay export or an automatic promotion workflow. On phones, test both portrait and landscape, including rotation while a menu is open. Short landscape drawers reserve actual space for map cards and camouflage swatches; detection and countdowns must leave touch controls usable. Automated layout checks cover 568×320, 667×375, 844×390, 932×430 and a 844×300 browser-chrome case, plus Chinese text. These checks supplement physical-device testing; they do not establish performance on every phone.

title: Film your own battles
text: Any battlefield, any tank and every effect the battle has, on a timeline you direct, taken away as stills or film.

title: Open the Studio
text: The Studio is the game's own film set, running in your browser. From the top bar Open Studio in the top bar to start a new scene. Open in Studio Every film on this site has Open in Studio: it stages that film as it was shot. Copy scene link A scene link carries the whole scene; opening it rebuilds that scene in your Studio. Films from this site Object 148 Proto, Tarkhan Steppe Leopard 2 Improved, Ruinspires M1A2 Abrams, Sirocco Wadi Challenger 1 Mk 2, Saltwind Narrows Stridsvagn 121, Frosthollow ZTZ-99 Longwei, Titan Gorge

title: Set the scene
text: Pick any battlefield, Olympus Basin and Earthrise Basin too, place tanks, aim their turrets and set their state. Time of day Dawn Morning Day Golden hour Sunset Dusk (blue hour) Night Tank states Intact Engine smoking Burning Wrecked Burnt-out wreck Turret blown off Frames 16:9 Film 9:16 Vertical 1:1 Square

title: Shots and the timeline
text: Add camera shots along the timeline; the camera moves from one to the next. Camera rigs Hero Tracking Rear chase Overhead Detail Lenses Wide · 58° Natural · 42° Tight · 28° Moves between shots Smooth Linear Cut Bézier Spline A sequence runs 1 to 20 s; a film up to 60 s. Speed ramps reach 8× for fast cuts and slow motion. Staged sequences Steel pursuit Track-level escort, a forward gun pass, then a rising battlefield reveal. Verdant Fields · Day · 8 s · 3 shots Desert crossfire A sunset engagement: approach, recoil and tracer, then the impact aftermath. Sirocco Wadi · Sunset · 8 s · 3 shots Coastal reconnaissance A moving coastal patrol with a rear follow, side portrait and sea-facing reveal. Saltmere Bay · Day · 8 s · 3 shots

title: Effects
text: Every effect is the battle's own, fired from the timeline at a tank, a point or a marker. Main gun shot Muzzle flash Tracer Impact Sparks Explosion Tank kill Dust burst Engine smoke Burning Track break Firing moment Frozen fireball Machine-gun burst Barrage Armour scars Exhaust belch Smoke screen Flare Embers Debris Shockwave Fire field

title: Stills and film
text: Take a still at any moment, or render the sequence to a film. Capture PNG saves the frame you see. Export film renders every frame offline with motion blur, drops none, and mixes in the battle's sound, as MP4 or WebM, whichever your browser encodes. Live recording captures the screen in real time instead. Size 1080p 1440p 2160p Rate 24 FPS 30 FPS 60 FPS Blur Off · 1 sample Draft · 4 samples Good · 8 samples Best · 16 samples Master · 32 samples Shake As authored Half Quarter Off

title: Save and share
text: Copy scene link: the scene travels inside the link. Save JSON downloads the scene file; Load JSON opens one. Slots keep scenes in this browser: click to load, Shift-click to save.

title: Fifty takes, filmed inside the game
text: The site's fifty takes, its portraits and its four films were shot in Scene Studio on the game's own maps, tanks and effects. Each take is code: staged by a search, judged as a schematic previz, reviewed in the engine, fixed at its source and rendered as a supersampled 4K final with its own sound.

title: Shots written as code
text: Every take on the site is a scene document, not a recording: the map, the time of day and the weather, the cast and its paint, each tank's route and speed, where each gun points, the camera's rail and the moment for its still. tools/media-r5/site50.mjs writes all fifty from one table, so a change to the plan reaches every take that shares it. The shot library keeps each take's scene exactly as the Studio saves it, so a take opens in the Studio from a link: the viewer below opens every featured take that way. The owner directs each round with notes: the lens on a three-dimensional track that swings close and far, tanks fast in every direction, fronts and quarters rather than rears, and a list of tanks that each lead a take of their own. Every round renders into folders of its own, so earlier versions stay beside the code that made them.

title: One take, every stage
text: Pick a take, then a stage. Round four is the loop delivered on 4 October, before the motion note. Engine review 1 is the first motion plan rendered small in the engine, with everything it caught. Previz is round six's plan as a schematic camera, and engine review 2 is that plan in the engine after the fixes. Engine review 3 is round seven: the plan re-staged on the 2.0 maps, the scenes the 4K finals render from.

title: The process
text: Ten steps take a shot from a note to the website. The checks run before any GPU time is spent, and every fix lands in the engine, the tools or the plan, never in a single frame.

title: Motion search and previz
text: The motion search staged all 50 site takes and all 165 fleet takes. For each take it tries road and open-ground routes, columns and fans of escorts, guns held on their own targets and lens moves by kind (a swoop, a lead reveal, an orbit that rises, a cable run, a weave, an overtake), and it scores every candidate for close-to-far range, climb, front angles, speed and flank swings. The winners are written to a tracked plan file. Previz draws each plan as a schematic camera's eye beside the map, with the lens's distance and height across the take. Choreography is judged here, in seconds per take, before a single frame is rendered.

title: The battlefield as the engine holds it
text: A survey of each map in the running game dumps every collision record (its footprint, height, crush threshold and canopy) with a 4 m grid of ground heights and water. An offline model rebuilds the battlefield from that dump and answers with the engine's own collision code. Routes are checked against it in 50 ms steps: a hull may crush what a battle hull would crush, and anything else fails the route, as does a start inside a building or a slope too steep to climb. The lens check samples the camera every 100 ms and casts five sightlines to the hero (its centre, nose, tail and both flanks) through every record and canopy; low cover never blocks, and a prop counts only when it is large on screen against the tank.

title: What the Studio gained
text: A spline camera rail keeps fast moves smooth through every key. Each tank drives its own route at speed with its gun stabilised on a target, and a travel frame lets the lens ride a swerving tank without swinging with it. The Plan view shows the take from above (every route, the camera's track and view, the lens's distance and height) and scrubs with the timeline. Tanks on the timeline now crush what they overrun, by the battle's own rule: a hull fells a fence, a wall or a tree when it runs over it faster than that object gives way. The crushes are planned from the routes before playback, fire live as the timeline plays and replay settled after a seek, so any frame shows the same wreckage. At night the Studio's camera holds a moonlit exposure, 1.25 stops under the map's, instead of adapting the dark back toward day.

title: The engine review
text: All fifty takes were rendered small in the game engine before any final. The first review caught three things the schematic could not: tanks driving through intact props in about half the takes, props in front of the lens in six, and eight night takes lit like day under a starry sky. Each fix went to its source: the Studio's crushes, the battlefield model and its lens check, and the night camera. The second review renders every take again at 960 pixels with a light probe on each. When the 2.0 maps changed the battlefields, the motion search re-staged the takes the new layouts broke, and a third review rendered all fifty on them before the finals start.

title: 4K finals and stills
text: Finals render at 3840 × 2160 and 30 frames per second, in deep focus: sharp from the lens to the horizon, with no depth-of-field blur in front of the tanks. Each frame is the average of 8 to 48 complete renders at sub-pixel offsets across a 60° shutter; fast motion adds renders until neighbouring ones are at most 1.5 pixels apart. The jittered average replaces the game's temporal anti-aliasing, bloom and the grade run once on the average, and a sharpening pass finishes the frame. Each take also renders two 4K stills at a 2 ms exposure: its key moment and a close portrait where the tank is largest on screen, each chosen with the whole tank in frame, centred, nothing in front of it and no burst of dust just before. About a hundred stills become posters, key art and social images; the films' ProRes masters are kept, and the site's formats are encoded from them.

title: Sound
text: Nothing in the films' sound is synthesized. The battle effects are the game's own recordings, placed from each cut's edit list with the engine's resolvers (the gun's class, the engine family, the track set, the map's echo tail and its ambience), and the hero's crew calls its shots on the radio, in its own language, over the engine's intercom chain. The score is generated with Eleven Music from a composition plan written from the cut's cue sheet. Its hits (braams in the sheet's chords, a sub boom, risers, a reverse swell and taiko) are generated sound effects, several takes each; the best measured take is kept and placed on its downbeat. Each film is mastered to −14 LUFS.

title: The films and the board
text: Four films are cut from the takes as HyperFrames compositions: a trailer, a 30-second cut, a 15-second vertical and the lineup. Their edit lists are generated from the takes, and the HTML compositions render frame-exact to video. The owner reviews every round on one board: each take's frames, previz, engine reviews and finals side by side, with the receipts of every change. Notes go back into the plan, the engine or the tools, and the next round renders beside the last.

title: The pictures
text: Every picture filmed for the game, grouped by what it shows: battle scenes by battlefield, vehicles by country, duels, firefights, gameplay, key art, the battlefields and the interface. Pick a collection, then any picture to open it.
